title: Technology: Banks urge sovereign AI capacity
full_text:
The country's largest banks say bringing the world's most powerful artificial intelligence models to train and run in Australian data centres must be a key part of the Albanese government's strategy, warning that economic gains from the powerful technology will otherwise accrue overseas.
Appearing at a parliamentary inquiry on Friday afternoon, Westpac chief AI officer Dan Jermyn said investing in "long-term sovereign AI capacity" should be "at the centre of Australia's AI strategy", amid concerns that much of the benefits of the new tools would instead flow to the United States.
"Countries that build capability across strategically important parts of the AI value chain will be better placed to capture economic benefits, attract investment and strengthen resilience," Jermyn said.
The comments from Jermyn and Pete Steel, National Australia Bank's executive overseeing AI, at the inquiry came as the government considers how to regulate data centres and the frontier developers of AI models, including OpenAI and Anthropic, which is behind Claude.
Earlier this week, Assistant Minister for Technology Andrew Charlton said voluntary regulations and industry codes would not be enough to oversee a growing AI industry, but harsh laws could drive companies away.
Steel told the inquiry that operating data centres and training frontier models in Australia would provide "critical mass to then enable sovereignty to become a reality, and to run things locally, sustainably".
"Australia should be more than a destination for AI built elsewhere. History tells us that economies which adopt transformational technology with energetic aspiration ultimately outperform those that invent it," he said.
Earlier in the week, Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn told the same committee - which will make recommendations to government by the end of next month - that Australia could become a trusted regional base for AI compute and intelligence production.
In its submission to the inquiry, the country's largest lender said developing capabilities in Australia would shape national security and economic resilience and avoid dependence or coercion from other countries.
"Training-grade infrastructure can enable Australian organisations to train and adapt advanced models using local data and expertise, particularly as powerful open-weight models become more widely available," it read.
But as the government considers tougher regulation on frontier models - after OpenAI agents hacked government systems - lenders say they should be able to operate under a carve-out from any laws to ensure they can keep using the cutting-edge tools needed for detecting scams, fraud and financial crime without having to disclose how the systems operate.
"The only effective response to AI used at scale against Australians is AI used at scale in their defence," Australian Banking Association chief executive Simon Birmingham said. "Australia cannot opt out. The question is whether we shape it with confidence or leave others to shape it for us."
Fears about AI safety have heightened over the past few months after OpenAI revealed that during testing one of its advanced models hacked into open-source coding platform Hugging Face, and in another incident broke into an Australian government website to obtain aggregated Medicare data.
Jason Kwon, chief strategy officer at OpenAI, used his appearance before the parliamentary inquiry to reiterate the company's apology for the Medicare hack, conceding it should have handled its response better.
Kwon said OpenAI has introduced additional monitoring processes that can notify people if an AI agent is doing something it is not supposed to, and promised the company would do better to disclose incidents in the future.
OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman and Elon Musk, the chief executive of xAI, which owns the Grok platform, last month rallied around a call from Anthropic's Dario Amodei to slow AI's development, after warnings by researchers who quit the industry.
